newsitem.title: USA: Lead battery must smarten up to survive in EVs.
newsitem.headline: Lead battery must smarten up to survive in EVs.

text.p: Lead-acid batteries, the cornerstone of metal demand, face stiffer competition from rival packs to power electric vehicles but cost will be the driving factor, the U.S. Lead Industries Assocation was told.
"Most car manufacturers today have abandoned lead-acid batteries in their (electric) vehicles," David Goldstein of the Electric Vehicle Association of Greater Washington DC said.
"But people don't recognise the cost of the other batteries. The cost issue is going to be a major determinant."

The lead battery was still far cheaper than nickel metal hydride or other rival batteries for EVs, and it could incorporate electronics to improve battery range, reliability and life cycle and still be cheaper, Goldstein said.
Several of the big U.S. and foreign car makers have or are about to launch purpose built EVs, all equipped with lead acid batteries so far, but nickel metal hydride will be used soon in some models.
Last month General Motors said it would equip some of its new EV1 cars with nickel metal hydride batteries instead of lead-acid counterparts in order to improve mileage between recharging.

To continue powering electric vehicles, the lead-acid battery must get smart and copy its computer-clad lithium ion rival unveiled last year by the Japanese, Goldstein said in a panel presentation on electric vehicles.
"This is a very significant trend that we have not yet matched in lead acid," Goldstein said.

The Freedonia Group has forecast that in the U.S. EV production will reach 40,000 units in 2000, rising to 320,000 units by 2005, but Goldstein stressed that it was impossible to accurately predict numbers at present.
"The oil industry is the leading organization trying to kill the electric vehicle," Goldstein said.
Steve Wilkinson, general manager, marketing of Cominco Metals, added: "There needs to be continued lobbying (of EVs) because there is a lot of lobbying on the other side by the petroleum companies."

But the lead-acid battery must be improved, such as speeding up recharging. Lead producer Cominco was this week given a grant by the Advanced Lead Acid Battery Consortium to find ways of improving charging times.
"This helps us defend our SLI (starter light ignition) market (in gas-powered cars) which is coming under threat as we try to lighten cars," Wilkinson said.
Michael Deelo, sales manager of Doe Run Co, a lead producer, said batteries accounted for 86 percent of U.S. annual lead consumption of 1.6 million tons.
Any increase in lead demand for EV batteries will have to be met by extra secondary metal production as primary lead output will decline from the turn of the century, Deelo said.

"Most of lead mine production is a byproduct of zinc and the lead to zinc ratio has been changing over the last ten years and it's been away from lead," Deelo said. "This is a trend we in the industry have to take a serious look at. Recycling will be the name of the game."
